summary: Defines the audio/L16 MIME type, a reasonable-quality audio format for use in Internet applications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Audio/L16 is a MIME label for uncompressed audio represented by 16-bit samples. The sender identifies the sample rate and may specify how many channels the data contains.

how to send uncompressed audio over internet
subtitle: The audio/L16 MIME type labels uncompressed, 16-bit audio with configurable rate and channels.

tldr.problem: The RFC says the set of IETF-standard audio MIME types was small and did not provide the higher-rate linear audio needed by some applications.
tldr.mechanism: Audio/L16 labels uncompressed audio using 16-bit signed two's-complement samples in network byte order, with registered sample rates and an optional channel count.
tldr.outcome: The registration gives applications a shared MIME type and parameters for identifying this audio data.

today: RFC 2586 is an Informational memo with no update or replacement listed in the unit metadata. It registers the audio/L16 MIME type and specifies its parameters.

sections.title: Why Register Audio/L16
sections.content:
RFC 2586 defines the audio/L16 MIME type for Internet applications. It says the then-current set of IETF-standard audio MIME types was small and that the existing types used an 8000-sample-per-second rate or LPC encoding.

The RFC presents audio/L16 as a simple registration for higher-rate, linear-encoded audio with multiple channels. It names email, web-served content and file uploads as possible uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds a standard label for a simple form of uncompressed audio. It is intended for applications that need sample rates and channel counts beyond the limited types discussed in the memo.

sections.title: Audio Data and Channels
sections.content:
Audio/L16 uses the L16 format described in RFC 1890: uncompressed audio stored as signed 16-bit values in two's-complement notation and network byte order. The MIME header gives the sample rate and can give the number of channels.

For multiple channels, channel numbers run from left to right starting at one, and samples are interleaved in channel order. For more than two channels, the RFC points to the AIFF-C convention for channel notation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each audio sample is a signed 16-bit number. With multiple channels, the data alternates between channels in their numbered order.

sections.title: MIME Registration Parameters
sections.content:
The registered media type is audio/L16. Its required rate parameter accepts 8000, 11025, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100 or 48000 samples per second.

The optional channels parameter states how many audio streams are interleaved and defaults to 1. The data is binary; for email, the RFC says Base64 encoding is suitable. It also lists compatibility with WAV and AIFF encoding and with the programs sox and rateconv.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIME header must state one of the registered sample rates. It can also state the number of channels; if it does not, the value is one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says audio data is believed to offer no security risks. It also notes that a multichannel transmission could be used to construct confusing messages when different users select different channels, and that the format can be used to hide data through steganography.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says audio itself is believed to pose no security risk, but also notes that audio channels could be used to hide data or create confusing messages.

references.text: Schulzrinne, H., "RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences with Minimal Control", RFC 1890, January 1996.
